query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the Al content in a mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMn HEA leads to the formation of a dense, continuous Al2O3-rich protective oxide layer that suppresses the formation of porous Mn-rich oxide scales.
generation.material_initial_state: A mechanically alloyed equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn HEA with a baseline low-Al content (e.g., ~5 at.% Al) exhibiting mixed oxide growth.
generation.intervention: Increase the Al content incrementally to ≥10 at.% while keeping other elemental ratios constant.
generation.conditions: Isothermal oxidation in air at 800 °C for up to 100 hours.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a thin (~1 μm), continuous, and dense Al2O3-rich oxide scale covering the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Higher Al content promotes the nucleation and growth of a slow-growing but highly stable alumina layer that effectively inhibits both oxygen ingress and outward diffusion of other elements, thereby suppressing formation of non-protective, porous manganese oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: The high-Al alloy will display logarithmic oxidation kinetics with significantly reduced mass gain (<5 g/m²) and thinner oxide layers relative to the low-Al baseline, which exhibits parabolic kinetics and porous, thicker oxide scales (≈25 μm).
generation.baseline: The low-Al HEA with predominantly Mn-rich oxide scale formation and higher mass gains during oxidation at 800 °C.
generation.boundary: This mechanism applies under controlled oxidation conditions in air at intermediate temperatures (around 800 °C) and may vary if other competing alloying effects become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Al concentration for balancing oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity is not precisely known; interactions with minor elements could introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two HEA compositions identical except for Al content (one with low Al (~5 at.%) and the other with high Al (≥10 at.%)). Subject both to oxidation at 800 °C for 100 hours.
measurements: Measure oxidation kinetics via weight gain analysis.
Characterize oxide scale structure and thickness using SEM, TEM, and XRD.
Assess oxide scale continuity and porosity using cross-sectional imaging.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased Al alloy does not show a continuous, thinner, and predominantly Al2O3-rich oxide scale with lower mass gain compared with the baseline, the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.3. Thermal Stability and High-Temperature Oxidation
cited_evidence.text: The high-temperature oxidation at 800 °C was evaluated based on the weight gains of the initially weighted sample with a defined surface. As one can see in Figure 14, the Mn15Al5 alloy showed a sort of parabolic kinetics of oxidation, which is known for rapid weight gain in a matter of minutes and slowing down over time due to the diffusion-driven character of oxygen transport through the developing oxide layer. However, as the annealing prolonged, the oxidation kinetics showed rather a linear mechanism according to the weight gains, suggesting the poor protective behavior of such layer due to, e.g., cracking or formation of pores within the layer. On the other hand, increasing the Al content resulted in logarithmic kinetics of oxidation, suggesting the creation of a dense protective layer, which did not tend to chip off over the time of annealing. Both the Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15 alloys gained less than 5 g m−2 of newly formed oxides after 100 h annealing at 800 °C. Similar behavior was also reported in the work of Lyu et al. [], who prepared the CoCrFeNiAlx (x = 0.1, 0.5, 1) alloy using vacuum arc melting, which significantly improved its oxidation resistance from 2 at.% of Al. The

The oxidation kinetics changed according to the content of Al initially from a parabolic (Mn15Al5) to a logarithmic (Mn10Al10 and Mn5Al15) rate, caused by the formation of a protective layer of Al2O3 instead of the MnxOy oxidic layer observed in the case of the first-mentioned alloy. Moreover, the sub-surface oxidation and porosity caused by the Mn diffusion toward the oxide layer were completely suppressed from 10 at.% of Al, reducing the overall thickness of the oxide layer from ≈25 μm (Mn15Al5) down to ≈1 μm. Considering the above-stated, changing the content of Al can be used for precise tailoring of the complex performance of the prepared alloys to achieve desired properties not only at the laboratory but also at elevated temperatures.

papers.title: An oxidation resistant refractory high entropy alloy protected by CrTaO4-based oxide.
papers.system: Refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NV1 alloy with adjusted Ti content)
papers.approach: Experimental oxidation testing at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for extended durations (up to 200 hours) with thermogravimetric analysis, XRD and microstructural characterization
papers.findings: NV1 alloy exhibited lower weight gain at high temperatures; at 1100 °C a protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer (with dispersed Al2O3 and Cr2O3) formed and improved oxidation resistance compared to similar alloys with higher Ti content.
papers.mechanism: Reduced Ti content promotes the preferential formation of a continuous CrTaO4-based layer that hinders both the outward diffusion of substrate elements and the inward diffusion of oxygen; controlled kinetics govern whether a protective oxide forms.

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) in both air and low oxygen partial pressure conditions for real-time phase and oxide evolution
papers.findings: A graded oxide layer forms with an outer Mn-rich oxide and inner Cr-rich oxide; however, classical protective Cr2O3 is not observed. Instead, manganese oxides (e.g., Mn2O3 transforming to Mn3O4) dominate, elucidating the influence of differential element diffusion.
papers.mechanism: The sequence of oxide formation is governed by the relative elemental diffusion rates (Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni) and differential oxygen affinity, affecting the kinetics of oxide layer development and its protective quality.

papers.title: Oxidation Behavior of Refractory AlNbTiVZr0.25 High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation tests at temperatures from 600 °C to 900 °C, with analysis by XRD and SEM to identify oxide phases and morphology
papers.findings: At lower temperatures (600–700 °C) oxidation showed a two-stage kinetics, shifting to nearly linear oxidation at 800 °C and catastrophic disintegration at 900 °C; various complex oxides including TiNb2O7, AlNbO4, and Nb2Zr6O17 formed.
papers.mechanism: Multiple mechanisms may be activated including formation of protective phases (AlNbO4) versus formation of porous, poorly protective oxides at higher temperatures, with Fickian diffusion of oxygen and alloying element redistribution playing key roles.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.approach: Mesoscale modeling using a stochastic Cellular Automata framework that integrates thermodynamics, kinetics, and microstructural features; simulation compared against experimental oxidation data
papers.findings: The simulation illustrated that for a single-crystal motif, oxide growth involves primarily α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 formation; however, with phase-segregated microstructures, a coexisting separation of oxide scales emerges.
papers.mechanism: Oxide scale growth is controlled by diffusion processes through the alloy’s microstructure; the interplay between thermodynamics (stable oxide phases) and kinetics (grain-boundary versus lattice diffusion) dictates the development of protective versus non-protective scales.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with refined microstructure
papers.approach: Experimental processing via stationary friction processing to obtain ultrafine-grained microstructure, followed by isothermal oxidation tests at 850–1050 °C, with kinetic analysis and oxide scale cross-sectional imaging
papers.findings: Samples with ultrafine grains (down to 0.43 μm) exhibited reduced oxidation kinetics (12–48% lower mass gains) and developed continuous protective oxide scales predominantly composed of chromia and alumina; enhanced grain boundary density promoted dense, protective layered oxide formation.
papers.mechanism: Reduction of grain size increases effective diffusion pathways via grain boundaries, which accelerates the formation of a continuous, protective oxide layer (first chromia then an Al-rich layer) that serves as an effective diffusion barrier against oxygen ingress.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Combined experimental techniques including in situ atom probe tomography, TEM, and X-ray absorption near-edge structure techniques to follow oxidation-induced surface changes in a controlled oxygen environment
papers.findings: Initial oxide formation is governed by atomic sizes and redox potentials with a subsequent inversion of composition; formation sequences transition from early chaotic oxidation to later structured, layered oxide films.
papers.mechanism: Selective oxidation is driven by the interplay of element-specific redox potentials, diffusivities, and cohesive energies; for instance, elements like Al and Cr form slower-growing, stable oxides that eventually dominate the protective scale formation, whereas more reactive elements such as Mn form non-protective oxides.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: Mechanically alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X HEAs with varying Al content
papers.approach: Systematic variation of Al content, followed by high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., at 800 °C for up to 100 hours), with phase identification and cross-sectional metallography
papers.findings: Lower Al alloys showed parabolic oxidation kinetics with thick, porous oxide layers and significant sub-surface oxidation, whereas higher Al content alloys (≥10 at.%) formed very thin, dense, protective Al2O3-rich layers with logarithmic kinetics.
papers.mechanism: Increased Al content promotes the formation of a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 scale that suppresses both oxygen ingress and element outward diffusion, serving as an effective passivation layer; conversely, lower Al levels favor non-protective Mn-oxides and increased porosity.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA processed by 3D laser printing
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation experiments at 700 °C and 900 °C with kinetic analysis and structural characterization of oxide layer formation
papers.findings: The alloy exhibited parabolic oxidation kinetics with formation of spinel-type oxides; at higher temperature and longer exposure, oxide exfoliation and substrate segmentation were observed, indicating compromised protective behavior.
papers.mechanism: Competing diffusion rates among alloying elements result in the formation of multi-component spinel oxides; however, the lack of a stable, continuous protective scale (such as continuous Al2O3 or Cr2O3) leads to degradation at very high temperatures.

established: High-entropy alloys can form protective oxide scales (e.g., CrTaO4, Al2O3, Cr2O3) that reduce oxidation rates at high temperatures.
Oxidation kinetics in HEAs are diffusion controlled, often following parabolic or logarithmic rate laws, depending on oxide scale integrity.
Elemental diffusion rates and alloy microstructure (grain size, phase separation) critically influence the formation and stability of protective oxide layers.

approaches_tried.approach: Adjusting alloy composition (e.g., reducing Ti or increasing Al content) to promote formation of protective oxides
approaches_tried.outcome: Improved oxidation resistance via formation of continuous, protective oxide scales (e.g., CrTaO4-based or Al2O3-rich layers)

approaches_tried.approach: Microstructural refinement (ultrafine grains via friction processing)
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced grain boundary diffusion led to the rapid establishment of protective oxide layers, reducing oxidation kinetics by 12–48%

approaches_tried.approach: Mesoscale modeling of oxidation using stochastic Cellular Automata
approaches_tried.outcome: Reproduced the effect of complex chemistry and microstructure on oxide growth, though the model highlighted limitations in capturing grain-boundary effects

mechanisms: Selective oxidation governed by differential elemental diffusion rates and redox potentials leading to the formation of specific protective oxide phases.
Protective behavior arises when slower oxidizing elements (e.g., Al and Cr) form dense, continuous oxide scales that act as diffusion barriers.
Microstructural factors such as grain size and phase distribution modify effective diffusion coefficients, influencing oxide growth kinetics.
disagreements: Whether the protective oxide is predominantly a simple scale (like continuous Cr2O3 or Al2O3) versus complex, multi-phase oxides (e.g., CrTaO4-based, mixed spinels).
The role of minor alloying elements (e.g., Ti, Mn) in either promoting or hindering the formation of a protective oxide layer, given their potential to form non-protective, porous oxides.
open_questions: What are the precise controlling parameters (e.g., diffusivity, redox potential, cohesive energy) that dictate when a protective oxide layer will form versus a non-protective one?
How does long-term exposure (beyond 200 hours) affect the stability and integrity of the protective oxide scales?
What is the interplay between nitridation processes and oxidation resistance in these alloys, especially at high temperatures?
opportunities: Conduct controlled studies comparing alloys that differ only in one key parameter (e.g., Al content or grain size) to test the hypothesis that controlled diffusion rates govern protective oxide formation.
Combine microstructural refinement with targeted compositional adjustments (reducing elements that hinder protective scale formation) to optimize the kinetics of oxide scale formation.
Utilize in situ characterization techniques (e.g., HTXRD, atom probe tomography) over extended time scales to dynamically monitor oxide layer formation and validate mechanistic predictions.
Investigate the quantitative relationship between alloying element diffusivities and the onset of protective scale formation under various oxygen partial pressures and temperatures.

directions.direction: Adjust alloy composition by reducing Ti content to promote selective formation of a protective CrTaO4-based oxide scale.
directions.assessment: This direction directly targets observed differences in oxide scale chemistry; lower Ti content has been linked to denser, protective CrTaO4 formation (e.g., PMC6513993::web::015::discussion), and the mechanism is supported by diffusion‐kinetics considerations. It is experimentally feasible via compositional tuning and extended oxidation tests.

directions.direction: Increase the Al content in HEAs to favor the formation of continuous, dense Al2O3 scales over non‐protective Mn-rich oxides.
directions.assessment: This addresses the competitive oxidation behaviour by shifting the oxide chemistry toward a more stable, slower-growing alumina barrier (PMC9692591::web::026::4_conclusions). The mechanism of selective oxidation via redox potential and diffusion is well established, and controlled compositional studies are straightforward.

directions.direction: Refine the grain microstructure (e.g., via friction processing) to enhance grain boundary diffusion, thereby accelerating protective oxide scale formation.
directions.assessment: Ultrafine grains provide increased diffusion pathways that can promote rapid formation of continuous oxide layers (PMC9026100::web::017::oxidation_kinetics). This direction directly influences kinetics and is supported by experimental evidence; the comparison between as-cast and ultrafine-grained samples is feasible.

directions.direction: Control diffusion kinetics by tailoring the relative diffusion rates of key alloying elements (e.g., suppressing Mn diffusion relative to Cr and Al) to favor protective oxide scale development.
directions.assessment: This direction integrates the interplay of elemental diffusivities and redox potentials to explain the formation and retention of protective scales. Prior evidence from HTXRD and oxidation kinetics (PMC10384371::web::026::4_3_oxidation_in_air) supports this idea, and it can be tested via controlled oxygen partial pressure experiments.

directions.direction: In situ monitoring of oxide growth using HTXRD and atom probe tomography to dynamically correlate phase evolution with oxidation resistance.
directions.assessment: While very informative and complementary to the above approaches, this direction is more about detailed characterization and may not directly test a single mechanistic hypothesis but rather yield dynamic insights.

re_retrieval.purpose: To identify evidence supporting or refuting the proposed hypotheses regarding the mechanisms and effects of alloy composition, microstructure, and processing methods on the oxidation resistance and mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys for high-temperature applications.
needs: Comparative data on both oxidation performance and mechanical properties for varying Al contents to optimize the protective oxide without sacrificing strength or ductility.
Further studies on the mechanical properties of high-Al HEAs to confirm that the increased Al content does not compromise mechanical integrity.
Further studies on the effects of Al content on the oxidation behavior and mechanical properties of HEAs.
Additional experimental/thermodynamic data or references measuring real-time oxide growth to confirm the extent and continuity of the CrTaO4 layer.
Additional studies on the mechanical properties of Ti-reduced refractory HEAs to ensure that the reduction in Ti does not compromise their structural integrity.
Further studies on the effects of Ti content on the oxidation behavior of refractory HEAs, particularly in relation to other alloying elements.
The hypothesis does not fully address the potential effects of Ti content on the oxidation behavior of the refractory HEA, particularly in relation to other alloying elements.
